inputs.need:
I am an emergency physician and the trauma lead for a rural emergency care network: three small hospitals and one regional ambulance service covering a large, sparsely populated area. Since 2023 our paramedics have carried tranexamic acid for adults with suspected major bleeding after injury, to be given within three hours of the injury. Nobody has checked how the pathway is working. Anecdotally, crews working alone or facing long drives give it less often, and some patients arrive at hospital more than three hours after injury without having received it, or receive it late, when it may do more harm than good.

I want to audit the pre-hospital tranexamic acid pathway: how many eligible patients receive it, how quickly, and whether the right patients get it. The ambulance service keeps every electronic patient care record in its database, and the three hospitals hold the outcomes. Ideally I would like to know whether patients who got the drug early did better, but the data-sharing agreement between the ambulance service and the hospitals lapsed this summer and I do not know when it will be renewed. I am not sure what kind of study this should be: a check against the pathway standard, a look at outcomes, or both. We have no funding, the ambulance service's audit team can pull the records, and our clinical governance meetings are the natural place to report. I would like a design that is honest about what we can and cannot conclude with the data we are allowed to use.
inputs.constraints: No funding; the work fits existing clinical governance time. Ambulance records can be reviewed only by the ambulance service's audit team. Hospital outcome data cannot be linked until a data-sharing agreement is in place.
localFacts: The ambulance service's clinical audit committee approved an audit of the pre-hospital tranexamic acid pathway on 14 August 2026 (reference CA-EMS-2026-22).
The data-sharing agreement between the ambulance service and the network's three hospitals (DSA-2023-04) expired on 30 June 2026 and has not been renewed.
The network's three emergency departments received 1,480 trauma patients by ambulance in 2025.

records.title: Pre-hospital tranexamic acid in a rural ambulance service: eligibility, administration and delays in a retrospective records review
records.abstract: We reviewed electronic patient care records for 612 adults who met a rural ambulance service's criteria for tranexamic acid after injury over three years. Fifty-eight percent received tranexamic acid before hospital arrival, at a median of 52 minutes after injury. Administration was less common when a single paramedic attended (41 percent) and for patients aged over 65 (49 percent). Eleven percent of those treated received the drug more than three hours after injury, against the protocol. Records did not always state the time of injury, which was estimated for 18 percent of patients. Hospital outcomes were not available.

records.title: Timing of tranexamic acid after injury and death from bleeding: a systematic review of individual patient data
records.authors: Oduya-Brennan K, Lefevre-Mahlangu T, Ishikawa-Doherty P
records.abstract: We pooled individual data on 38,900 bleeding patients from randomised trials of tranexamic acid. Immediate treatment reduced the odds of death from bleeding by about 70 percent, and the benefit fell by about 10 percent for every 15 minutes of delay, with no benefit seen after three hours. There was no increase in vascular occlusive events overall. Most participants were treated in hospital, and few trials recorded the time of pre-hospital administration, so the effect of delays before arrival is inferred from in-hospital timing.

records.title: Linking ambulance and hospital records for trauma outcome audit: matching rates and pitfalls
records.abstract: We linked ambulance patient care records to emergency department and inpatient records in one region using date of birth, sex, postcode and arrival time. Linkage matched 91 percent of trauma patients conveyed directly but only 78 percent of those transferred between hospitals, and matching was lower for patients with missing identifiers at the scene. Unmatched patients were more often older, more severely injured and transferred. The authors warn that outcome audits based on linked data will overrepresent less severely injured patients unless unmatched records are followed up by hand, which requires a data-sharing agreement covering all sites.

records.title: Thromboembolic events after pre-hospital tranexamic acid in older trauma patients: a registry analysis
records.authors: Pellegrini-Achterberg M, Sato-Okafor L, Dunmore-Reyes A
records.abstract: Using a regional trauma registry, we compared 1,020 patients aged 65 or over who received pre-hospital tranexamic acid with 1,540 who did not. Venous thromboembolism within 30 days was recorded in 3.1 and 2.4 percent respectively (adjusted odds ratio 1.21, 95 percent CI 0.78 to 1.88). Mortality did not differ after adjustment for injury severity and anticoagulant use. Treated patients were more severely injured, and the registry captured only patients admitted to trauma units, so the analysis may miss events after discharge or among patients managed in smaller hospitals.

records.title: Why paramedics withhold tranexamic acid in rural trauma: a qualitative study of decision-making
records.abstract: We interviewed 24 paramedics from two rural ambulance services about recent trauma calls in which tranexamic acid was or was not given. Paramedics described three main reasons for withholding it: uncertainty about the time of injury, the workload of a single-crew response while managing the airway and bleeding, and worry about giving it to older patients taking anticoagulants. Several said they would give it more readily with a checklist prompt on the electronic patient care record. Paramedics rarely learned what happened to their patients after handover, which they felt made it hard to judge whether their decisions were right.

response.synthesis: Five retrieved records from the fixture search, appraised at abstract level; a second search channel failed and returned nothing. Paramedics describe uncertain injury times, single-crew workload and concern about anticoagulated older patients as reasons for withholding the drug. In one rural service, a little over half of eligible patients received pre-hospital tranexamic acid and one in nine doses was late. Pooled trial data show the benefit falls with every 15 minutes of delay and is absent after three hours. Linking ambulance to hospital records misses more of the older, more severely injured and transferred patients, and a registry of older patients shows a small, imprecise excess of thromboembolism.
response.gradeRationale: High certainty about the timing effect from pooled trials, but low certainty for the questions this network would answer: compliance and outcomes in rural pre-hospital care rest on single observational studies with missing data and selection by linkage.
response.summary: Five retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims; overall certainty low for the local questions.

response.title: Pre-hospital tranexamic acid in a rural emergency network: an audit of eligibility, administration and timing
response.abstract: Aim: to measure how many eligible injured adults receive pre-hospital tranexamic acid within three hours of injury in a rural ambulance service. Methods: audit of ambulance patient care records from January 2023 to June 2026 against the pathway standard, with second-reviewer checks of eligibility. Results and conclusions will be written after the audit; no outcome analysis is included.
response.introduction: Tranexamic acid reduces death from bleeding when given early, and the benefit falls with delay. Rural crews face long transport times and often work alone, and the network has never audited its pathway.
response.methods: Eligible incidents were identified from the ambulance records database; administration, dose time and injury time (known or estimated) were coded, with a second reviewer checking 10 percent of eligibility decisions. Results are proportions with confidence intervals by crew configuration, age and transport time.
response.results: No records have been reviewed yet. The report will present eligible incidents, the proportion treated within three hours, time to dose, doses outside protocol and documentation of injury time.
response.discussion: The discussion will describe where the pathway fails and what support might help, and will state that effects on survival cannot be judged without linked hospital data.
response.limitations: Record quality, estimated injury times and the absence of outcomes.
response.conclusion: To be written after the audit; it will be limited to compliance and timing.
